changes.summary: To mark the centenary of the death of Claude Monet (1840-1926), the Musée d’Orsay is joining forces with the Artizon Museum and the Nikkei in Tokyo to present an exceptional exhibition titled “Monet. Le paysage en question / Monet. A question of landscape”. This major international event brings together over a hundred of the artist’s and his contemporaries’ masterpieces, almost fifty of which will be lent by the Musée d’Orsay for an unprecedented visit to Japan. It marks the official launch of commemorations devoted to the centenary of Monet’s death, which will take place in France and across the world in 2026. The exhibition provides an exploration of Monet’s body of work in terms of nature and landscape. Nature is omnipresent, nourishing his work as a landscape painter, structuring his artistic approach and guiding his life. From the 1850s to his death, Monet spent his time tirelessly depicting forests and trees, flowers and cliffs, rivers, seas, skies and clouds, composing almost 1,800 landscapes in the course of over seventy years of continuous creation. His travels – Paris region, Normandy, the South, Brittany, England, the Netherlands and Norway – and the gardens he laid out in Argenteuil, Vétheuil and finally in Giverny became so many reinvented landscapes; according to Proust, the garden and water lily ponds are works “painted directly from nature”. Hence, landscape seems to have been a favored means of expression, a real laboratory in which Monet redefines our relationship with art and the world. The exhibition takes a closer look at what these landscapes reveal in an attempt to shed light on Monet’s “nature” in the age of industrialization. A “love of nature” was at the origin of his vocation. He was tireless in his assertion of it and it became a way of seeing, feeling and making an evolving truth perceptible while observing the increasing effects of industrialization.
